analysis.one_liner: Bans brand drug companies from paying generic or biosimilar makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: Introduced in December 2018 by a Democrat and a Republican, the bill was sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never received a committee vote, and died when that Congress ended three days into 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic or biosimilar maker is sued over a patent, the brand company sometimes settles by paying the challenger to stay off the market for years — a deal known as a "pay-for-delay" settlement. This bill would tell the Federal Trade Commission to treat such deals as presumptively anticompetitive, with exceptions for genuine litigation-expense payments (capped at $7.5 million), early-entry licenses, and covenants not to sue. Companies that broke the rule would face civil penalties up to triple the value of the deal, and violators could also lose the 180-day exclusivity period that rewards a first generic challenger.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and health payers, including federal programs that fund more than 40 percent of retail drug spending, who would get access to generic and biosimilar competition sooner. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers gain access to markets they are currently paid to avoid.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that generic drugs cost 80 to 85 percent less than brand-name drugs, but only 28 percent of drug spending is generic, and that settlements in which brand companies pay potential competitors have unduly delayed low-cost generics.
It lets the FTC presume that a settlement paying a generic or biosimilar applicant for delaying its entry is anticompetitive, shifting the burden to the companies to prove the deal is lawful.
Violating companies face civil penalties up to three times the value they received, and a first generic challenger whose agreement violates the law would forfeit its 180-day exclusivity reward.
Biological drugs make up more than 40 percent of prescription drug spending, so extending the ban to biosimilar settlements targets the highest-cost segment of the market.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies, which could no longer preserve monopoly profits by sharing them with would-be generic and biosimilar challengers, and generic firms that receive settlement payments instead of competing.

drawbacks.text: The bill presumes every settlement in which a challenger receives anything of value and agrees to delay entry is anticompetitive, which can sweep in legitimate settlements and push patent disputes into expensive full litigation instead of negotiated resolution; companies must prove procompetitive benefit by clear and convincing evidence to escape liability.

The presumption may deter genuine procompetitive deals, such as settlements allowing early generic entry, since the bill expressly forbids the fact finder from presuming that an early-entry provision makes a deal procompetitive.
Exclusions such as the $7.5 million litigation-expense cap require case-by-case judgment, and critics could argue the FTC already has antitrust authority over these deals without a bright-line rule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — faster arrival of drugs costing 80 to 85 percent less than brand versions — is large and well documented in the bill's own findings. The main cost is fewer settled patent disputes and more full-scale litigation, which raises industry costs and some case outcomes would be harder to call. The design mitigates this with exclusions for early-entry licenses, capped litigation-expense payments, and covenants not to sue.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate received the bill and sent it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, but the committee never voted on it and the bill expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on December 19, 2018, with Senator Chuck Grassley joining as cosponsor — the only cosponsor listed.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action, hearing, markup, or vote is recorded in the action history.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and bills not enacted by then expire, so the measure never reached the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept the ability to settle patent disputes by paying generic and biosimilar challengers to delay market entry, preserving higher-priced monopolies for longer; generic firms that take settlement payments also kept that revenue stream. Patients paid longer for brand-priced drugs.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate on December 19, 2018.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.role: Senate Judiciary Committee chairman; cosponsor (the bill's only listed cosponsor)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, but as the committee to which it was referred held no markup or vote on it, and the bill never came to the floor.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.role: Companies whose patent settlements the bill targets
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed pay-for-delay bans, which would end the practice of paying generic challengers to stay off the market; no member of Congress formally opposed the bill in the record because it never advanced to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat and a Republican sponsored the bill together, so no party divide is visible; with no committee or floor votes, there was never a record of who would have supported or opposed it.

industries.note: The bill ends pay-for-delay settlements, which let these companies share monopoly profits with challengers to keep cheaper copies off the market; consumers pay brand prices for years longer as a result.

They would forfeit settlement payments from brand companies, but they gain earlier market entry, where generic versions sell at 80 to 85 percent below brand prices. Their product interests line up with patients' interests.

industries.industry: Biosimilar and interchangeable biological product makers
industries.note: The same ban applies to biologic patent settlements, cutting off delay payments but opening earlier entry into a segment that is more than 40 percent of drug spending.
